newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian King urges new start after child horrors.
newsitem.headline: Belgian King urges new start after child horrors.

text.p: King Albert appealed on Tuesday to the Belgian people to make a new start after more than four months of revelations of child sexual abuse, murder and official bungling that have shaken their faith in the state.

Albert, who sparked controversy over his constitutional role in September when he first began making statements about the scandal and meeting the parents of missing and dead children, pulled few punches in his Christmas address to the nation.
"Christmas is traditionally a time of family happiness. But this year we all still have in our hearts a profound wound that will not heal.
"The faces of Julie and Melissa, of An and Eefje, of Elizabeth, of Loubna Benaissa and the many other missing children are engraved on our memories," he said.

The affair came to light in mid-August with the arrest of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux followed by the rescue from a makeshift dungeon in his house of Sabine Dardenne and Laetitia Delhez -- both of whom had been sexually abused.

Two days later Dutroux led police to the bodies of eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo, buried in the garden of one of his six houses in and around the central Belgian city of Charleroi. The girls had starved to death.
Barely two weeks later Dutroux again led police to another house where they unearthed the bodies of teenagers An Marchal and Eefje Lambrecks.

The parents of the dead girls launched a campaign complaining at police and judicial bungling in the searches for their daughters. They were joined by the parents of other missing children including Elizabeth Brichet and Loubna.

"This national tragedy continues to distress us deeply. We did not think that such things could happen here, but it is the cruel truth," Albert said. "We must make sure that they can never happen again."
He listed numerous actions that needed to be taken.

Children's rights had to be respected and families should become more cohesive. There should be less violence in advertising, on television and in the cinema, which should also stop treating women as objects.
People should focus more on the simple things in life than on the single-mided pursuit of material wealth, and immigrant families should be welcomed into the community with open arms.

"We wish a more humane and more efficient justice," the King said. "We wish a country where the Flemish, the Walloons and the people of Brussels walk together, side by side as they did in the White March".
In October more than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in what came to be known as the White March -- the biggest peacetime demonstration of its kind in the country.
It was to show support and sympathy with the parents of the dead and missing chilrden, but rapidly turned into a demonstration of disgust at a system seen as deeply corrupt.
"We wish that all people in public positions of authority reintegrate with the population and consider themselves to be in its service," Albert said.
"We want a society where a new form of responsible citizenship develops and where everyone is involved," he said.
"These hopes of the vast majority of us can be made to come about if we all unite our efforts to turn our individual desires into a collective reality.

"Everyone must play their part. Doing it with a calm determination, in a constructive manner, but also without extremism or blind accusations. Remain vigilant but do not fall into a general climate of suspicion." Albert said.
